items.title: Ernest 'Punch' Miller Interview, 1960-04-04
items.q: I went to Natchez and played with this boy who got burned up, Walter Barnes. Played there for two, three years with him, and how lucky I was. Well he was the father there, see how he'd do, he'd go out in the winter

ctx.x: That's the way King Zulu was patterned his road, he's all over the city.

Yeah. Now they used to have a nice road, they used to come when they had the old basin, that Howard Avenue, Ramport, they used to come up there and come up in the boat, in the boat, you know. Come right to Ramport and Chewie and Howard Avenue in that big, what do you call it, a pond or a river or something there, and they'd get off there and get on the float, and go on down Ramport to Connelly. But after they closed that up, that killed their route, see. I want to ask you, did you ever play around Natchez much? I…
And he had a grocery store in Chicago. Yeah, a big grocery store.

items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: I went out two years with him like that, the same way I did with Walter Barnes. He'd go out for the winter all down Florida and everywhere.

ctx.x: Somebody once told me you worked with the Jelly Roll on the road.

Oh, yeah, I worked with Jelly. About, well, I went out two years with him. That's how I worked. See, Jelly, he would, in the wintertime, he'd take a band out. He'd go all over. Well, summer, he'd keep band together, but he wouldn't do much playing in the summer. But, I went out two years with him like that, the same way I did with Walter Barnes. He'd go out for the winter all down Florida and everywhere. But, when he'd come back, he had a big grocery in Chicago. Barnes, huh?
Barnes, Walter Barnes? Yeah, Walter Barnes.
